transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: Tue Jul 21 2026 15:00 PDT
Recorded at: 2026-07-21T15:00:00-07:00
Duration: 68 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE); Samir Patel (Redwood SE); Liam O'Connor (Redwood); Dana Morales; Ravi Kapoor; Elena Suarez; Mike Huang; Priya Nair
Shared artifacts: https://redwood.app/secure/onprem-checklist (Redwood private checklist), https://drive.oakridge/collab/network-reqs (customer proto), SOC2 attestation will be emailed

Summary (auto): Security deep-dive on private/VPC deployment. Focus was on egress lock-down, key management (KMS/HSM), audit log path to customer's SIEM, SSO/RBAC mapping, and policy for model fallback and logging. Action items recorded.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I think we got most of the folks, do we have anybody else?
[00:08] Dana Morales: Dana here from Cloud Ops, thanks Maya.
[00:10] Ravi Kapoor: Ravi, Security.
[00:12] Elena Suarez: Elena, compliance.
[00:14] Mike Huang: Mike, DevOps.
[00:16] Priya Nair: Priya from legal, hi.
[00:20] Maya Chen: Great, high level agenda — Samir will dig into the network flows and Liam will walk KMS/rotation and logging. We'll try to get to SSO and SOC2 questions.
[00:33] Samir Patel: Cool, so starting with the private deployment model — imagine a private control plane in your VPC that talks to the inference pods via internal endpoints, we recommend putting the pods in private subnets with no public IPs. There's a egress path through a NAT or egress gateway and optionally an egress proxy for allow-listing.
[00:47] Ravi Kapoor: Sorry, egress gateway — is that a managed appliance by Redwood or something we have to spin up?
[00:51] Samir Patel: Good q. For the private option Redwood provides a lightweight control-plane connector that forms an authenticated mTLS connection to your control plane; the data plane can be fully inside your VPC. The egress is your responsibility — we give IP ranges and we can either send traffic out via your NAT or you can route outbound through a dedicated egress proxy. That's the place you filter to your SIEM etc.
[01:10] Mike Huang: so to be clear, outbound calls to model variants or telemetry — they go through our egress, not Redwood's public NAT?
[01:14] Samir Patel: Yes, outbound flows exit from your VPC; Redwood won't source- NAT on our side unless you choose a hosted fallback. For private fully on-prem or VPC the egress stays local to you.
[01:26] Elena Suarez: On SOC2 note — we need evidence that audit logs and admin actions are captured and immutable, are you pushing to S3 or can we forward to Splunk directly?
[01:36] Liam O'Connor: We can stream audit logs to your SIEM. Typically we ship via secure syslog over TLS or use S3 with object lock if you want immutable retention. There is also an option for direct ingestion via our collector — we can push to an endpoint you provide. 
[01:52] Priya Nair: Object lock is interesting. Does Redwood control the KMS keys for that S3? We need clear separation of duties.
[01:58] Liam O'Connor: For private deployments you can bring your own KMS. Redwood supports AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, and HSM-backed keys via Cloud HSM. You hold the root keys in your KMS; Redwood's control plane uses a deployed service account to request short‑lived keys for runtime encryption. We do not retain customer master keys.
[02:18] Ravi Kapoor: Clarify "short lived" — is that per session? per container?
[02:22] Liam O'Connor: It's per workload credential; typically rotated every 12 hours and ephemeral per pod instance. We can tighten that if you want 1-hour rotation.
[02:29] Dana Morales: We had an internal requirement for key rotation every 24 hours, and HSM for keys used to encrypt logs that contain PII.
[02:36] Samir Patel: HSM option is supported — you'll need to configure a backend and grant the connector access. We'll include a step-by-step doc.
[02:42] Maya Chen: Quick aside on data residency — are you expecting model tokens or payloads to ever leave region?
[02:46] Ravi Kapoor: No, everything must stay in our us-east-1 tenancy.
[02:50] Samir Patel: No problem, we can pin model variants to region-local assets, and the control plane can be co-located. Fallback to hosted models would be disabled unless you explicitly allow.
[03:05] Mike Huang: About egress IPs, will Redwood give a stable list? We have strict firewall rules and can't open wide ranges.
[03:12] Samir Patel: Yes, for private deployments we provide a small set of CIDR ranges used by the control-plane connector. If you run in purely private mode those will be internal IPs. For any outbound third-party calls Redwood needs, we document them.
[03:25] Ravi Kapoor: I need specifics — like the /32s or exact endpoints we can add to our allow-list.
[03:31] Maya Chen: We'll provide a spreadsheet with IPs and FQDNs. Action item.
[03:34] Elena Suarez: On RBAC and SSO — mapping our teams to roles: we need separation between Admins who can change model pinning and Operators who can only deploy. How do you model RBAC?
[03:44] Liam O'Connor: Redwood has role-based controls with built-in roles and custom roles. For private customers you can map your SAML/Okta groups to those roles. We log role changes as part of the audit trail.
[03:54] Priya Nair: Does the SAML assertion include the user email that we can map to our internal IDs?
[03:58] Liam O'Connor: Yes, the assertion or SCIM sync includes email and group membership. There are occasionally mismatches in attribute names — we can script the transform.
[04:08] Dana Morales: About network segmentation — we want to put inference pods in isolated subnets with no egress except to the model cache tier and internal storage. Is the KV cache a network service?
[04:18] Samir Patel: The KV cache is an internal endpoint; it's either co-located with the pods or reachable via a VPC endpoint. You can lock it down using security groups. Note: sometimes people call it K-V cache, or key-value cache — we saw a doc that spelled it "K V cache" which is confusing.
[04:32] Mike Huang: If we pin models, disk artifacts stay in our storage?
[04:36] Samir Patel: In private deployments the model artifacts are cached inside your infra. We recommend using an EBS volume or networked filesystem accessible only to the inference pool.
[04:45] Ravi Kapoor: Logging PII: We want to ensure user input never lands in logs or if it does it's redacted. How does Redwood handle sensitive prompt data?
[04:54] Liam O'Connor: We have configurable scrubbers and configurable sampling for transcripts. By default we don't persist full request bodies in audit logs; we capture metadata and hashes. For the pilot we can enable stricter redaction and show you how it looks.
[05:08] Elena Suarez: Can you demonstrate the scrubber in a sandbox?
[05:11] Maya Chen: Yes that's part of the pilot scope.
[05:14] Samir Patel: Back to egress — typical patterns we see: 1) Strict NAT with firewall allow-listing; 2) Egress proxy that does TLS inspection and enforces FQDN allow-lists; 3) Private peering to partner endpoints for SIEM. For Oakridge I'd recommend pattern 2 or 3 depending on inspection needs.
[05:35] Mike Huang: Our security team prefers egress proxy with TLS termination for advanced DLP, can Redwood work with that?
[05:40] Samir Patel: Yes, Redwood supports proxy chaining. The connector will honor HTTP_PROXY/HTTPS_PROXY env vars and mTLS can be terminated at the proxy. There are occasional quirks with streaming responses; we'll validate during pilot.
[05:54] Ravi Kapoor: About firewalls — do you require any inbound rules? We try to avoid opening inbound except to bastion hosts.
[06:01] Samir Patel: For private deployments inbound is only from your internal bastions or service mesh; we don't require public inbound ports. The control plane initiates the connection to the connector. So no public inbound required.
[06:10] Dana Morales: And for monitoring, what signals do we get? metrics, traces, request ids?
[06:15] Liam O'Connor: We emit per-request telemetry, token counts, latency histograms, and a stable request-id propagated to logs. You can also enable sampling of complete transcripts for QA.
[06:26] Priya Nair: Liability question — if a user prompt leaks via logs, what's Redwood's position?
[06:32] Maya Chen: We'll cover contractual protections in the DPA and security addendum. For the pilot we'll keep logs in your SIEM.
[06:36] Elena Suarez: On retention — we need logs immutable for 3 years for certain audit trails. Is that feasible?
[06:41] Liam O'Connor: Yes, with S3 object lock or your SIEM retention policy you can meet that. We'll include recommended lifecycle configs.
[06:50] Samir Patel: Small gotcha: streaming and prefix caching can cause intermediate KV entries to be stored — we can configure TTLs. If you put a short TTL, you reduce cost but may increase cold starts.
[07:03] Mike Huang: What's the impact on latency if TTL is short?
[07:06] Samir Patel: Expect a cold-start penalty for first requests after eviction — maybe an extra 50–120 ms depending on model. We'll include benchmarks.
[07:15] Ravi Kapoor: We have one more question on FIPS/HSM: our auditors want FIPS-validated crypto for key ops. Does Redwood's HSM option meet FIPS?
[07:23] Liam O'Connor: The HSM providers we integrate with are FIPS-compliant. We'll document the specific modules and the scope. For some deployments we can provide logs of key metadata without exposing key material.
[07:36] Dana Morales: Can we run a short dry-run of failover? If a model variant is unhealthy, we want automatic fallback only after permission.
[07:44] Samir Patel: There are rollout policies — canary, A/B, and automatic fallback. In private mode we can set strict no-fallback unless explicitly allowed. We'll show the policy UI in the pilot.
[07:58] Mike Huang: Any special firewall rules for control-plane health checks?
[08:02] Samir Patel: Health checks are outbound from your control plane to our collector; they use mTLS on a small set of endpoints. We'll provide ports/URLs.
[08:15] Ravi Kapoor: On egress data to third-party telemetry (like to analytics), are there any calls by Redwood to third parties by default?
[08:21] Maya Chen: No, default is telemetry off for private deployments; any 3rd-party integrations are opt-in.
[08:30] Priya Nair: From legal perspective, can we have a clause forbidding Redwood from using prompt data for model training?
[08:36] Maya Chen: Yes, in enterprise DPA we carve out data usage — for private deployments we don't train on customer prompts unless authorized. We'll add explicit language.
[08:47] Elena Suarez: OK let's recap next steps.
[08:50] Maya Chen: Sure: Maya send SOC2 & deployment checklist; Samir network diagram and IP/CIDR spreadsheet; Liam KMS/HSM notes; Oakridge to deliver egress endpoints and SIEM details. Then pilot start early August.
[09:03] Ravi Kapoor: Sounds good.
[09:06] Samir Patel: I'll also attach sample firewall templates and an example NAT configuration.
[09:12] Mike Huang: Please include the streaming caveats — we had an issue once where long streaming sessions looked like DDoS to our IDS.
[09:19] Samir Patel: Good call — we'll include IDS tuning guidance.
[09:23] Priya Nair: Legal will expect the DPA and DSR response times — can you share a draft?
[09:28] Maya Chen: I'll include a DPA draft in the follow-up email.
[09:31] Elena Suarez: Thanks everyone.
[09:33] Maya Chen: Thanks all — we'll follow up with docs and schedule the pilot prep.

End of transcript.

Notes on transcription: occasional speaker labels and acronym spellings may be slightly off (e.g., K V cache vs KV cache, kuber-net-ees), filler words present.
